title: Direct identification of the child through account/device association when sending live GPS
description: The child’s device regularly sends precise live GPS coordinates to the backend. If the transmission is tied to an account, device identifier, phone number, or persistent app token, the act of sharing can directly identify the child as the subject of the location data.
assumptions: Assumes the GPS updates are authenticated or otherwise associated with a persistent user/device identity.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on standard LINDDUN identification decomposition; exact sub-node may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Disclosure of highly sensitive real-time location by the child device
description: By transmitting live GPS coordinates at regular intervals, the source discloses highly sensitive personal data. Real-time location can reveal home, school, routines, religious attendance, health visits, and other intimate aspects of the child’s life.
assumptions: Assumes coordinates are sufficiently precise and frequent to infer meaningful places and routines.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree sub-node may differ across LINDDUN Pro versions; applicability is strong.

title: Linkability of successive GPS updates on the data flow
description: Regular interval transmission of GPS coordinates creates a stream of observations that can be linked together as belonging to the same child/device/session. Even without explicit identity in payload, timing, routing, tokens, or pseudonymous identifiers can allow correlation of updates into a continuous movement trail.
assumptions: Assumes repeated transmissions carry stable metadata, session information, or are otherwise observable as belonging to the same sender.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; the core threat is strong because periodic location updates are inherently correlatable.

title: Identification via network and protocol metadata in transit
description: Data in transit may expose identifiers such as IP address, device identifiers, authentication tokens, or transport metadata that can identify the child or their household, even aside from the GPS payload itself.
assumptions: Assumes standard mobile networking where backend communications expose metadata to network observers or intermediaries.
uncertainty_note: Applies especially if transport metadata is visible to intermediaries; exact node id may vary.

title: Disclosure of location and movement patterns in transit
description: If the flow is observed in transit, the GPS payload and its timing can disclose the child’s current whereabouts and movement patterns. Even encrypted channels may still leak some sensitive information through metadata such as timing and frequency.
assumptions: Assumes an attacker or intermediary can observe the communication channel or its metadata.
uncertainty_note: Payload disclosure depends on transport protections; metadata-based disclosure remains plausible even with encryption.

title: Backend can link location updates over time into a persistent mobility profile
description: Upon receipt, the backend can aggregate repeated GPS updates into a longitudinal record of the child’s movements. This enables linking visits, routines, and events across time, potentially across services or datasets if common identifiers are used.
assumptions: Assumes the backend stores or processes updates with a persistent identifier.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node may vary; threat clearly applies to backend aggregation of repeated location data.

title: Backend identifies the child from received live location data
description: The backend can identify the child by combining the incoming GPS stream with account records, device registration, parental account data, or other backend-held identifiers.
assumptions: Assumes the backend maintains user, device, or household records associated with the incoming data.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort; identification risk is strong given typical backend account linkage.

title: Backend learns sensitive facts from precise live GPS data
description: The backend’s receipt and processing of precise, frequent GPS coordinates can reveal sensitive facts about the child, such as home and school location, daily routines, social relationships, visits to clinics or places of worship, and periods of vulnerability.
assumptions: Assumes the backend retains enough precision and history to infer semantic locations and routines.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id may differ by version; disclosure/inference risk is clear.

title: Backend may process live child location in ways unexpected by the child
description: The child may not understand or reasonably expect the full extent of backend processing of continuous location updates, including analytics, profiling, retention, sharing, or secondary uses. This creates a threat that processing is not transparent or intervenable from the child’s perspective.
assumptions: Assumes limited child comprehension and/or insufficient just-in-time explanation of backend processing.
uncertainty_note: This is a genuine unawareness risk, especially for child users, but depends on the surrounding notice/UX design.

title: Backend collection of continuous child GPS data may exceed necessity or valid consent basis
description: Receiving live GPS coordinates at regular intervals for a child creates a risk that the processing is not compliant with data minimization, purpose limitation, retention limits, or child-consent/parental-authorisation requirements. Continuous precise tracking is particularly difficult to justify unless strictly necessary for the stated purpose.
assumptions: Assumes jurisdiction imposes privacy/data-protection obligations for children’s precise location data.
uncertainty_note: Compliance depends on jurisdiction, purpose, and controls; threat is plausible but context-sensitive.

title: Backend stores precise location pings beyond what is necessary
description: The backend writes each location ping to persistent storage, which can constitute avoidable disclosure of highly sensitive personal data if full precision, full frequency, or all pings are stored when the service only needs coarser, aggregated, or shorter-lived location data.
assumptions: Assumes the system may not strictly require retention of every raw location ping at full precision for its stated purpose.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selection is based on best judgement from LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimality concepts; the retrieved context did not provide a more specific node mapping for this exact case.

title: Stored location history enables linking of multiple pings to the same individual
description: Once the Location History Store receives and accumulates repeated pings, it can link records over time into a longitudinal movement history, allowing correlation of visits, routines, and co-location patterns for the same user or device.
assumptions: Assumes records contain a stable identifier, account reference, device identifier, or other correlatable attributes.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree node may vary depending on the project's threat-tree version; applicability of linkability is strong given persistent location-history storage.

title: Location history records may identify a user or device
description: Precise or repeated location pings stored in the destination data store can identify a person or device directly or indirectly, for example through home/work inference, unique mobility patterns, or association with account identifiers.
assumptions: Assumes the stored pings are precise enough, frequent enough, or associated with identifiers such that re-identification is feasible.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is best-effort; the identification risk itself is well supported for persistent location histories.

title: Stored location history allows inference of sensitive activities and attributes
description: Processing or merely retaining detailed location history can reveal sensitive information such as home and workplace, religious attendance, medical visits, political participation, intimate relationships, habits, and daily routines.
assumptions: Assumes the store retains sufficiently granular historical location data over time.
uncertainty_note: Specific tree node chosen by best judgement; detectability/inference risk is strongly applicable to longitudinal location data.

title: Users may be unaware that every location ping is persistently stored
description: If the system stores each location ping in the Location History Store without clear notice, users may not understand the extent, granularity, retention, or downstream use of their location history.
assumptions: Assumes notice is incomplete, unclear, or not presented at the time location collection/storage occurs.
uncertainty_note: Unawareness depends on the surrounding UX and privacy notice, which are not described here.

title: Persistent storage of location history may exceed or diverge from user consent
description: Writing every location ping to the Location History Store may be non-compliant if consent was not obtained for continuous tracking, long-term retention, precise storage, or secondary uses beyond the original purpose.
assumptions: Assumes consent or another lawful basis may be absent, insufficiently specific, or not aligned with this storage practice.
uncertainty_note: Compliance depends on the actual legal basis, consent wording, retention policy, and jurisdiction, none of which are provided.

title: Backend shares more precise location data than necessary for geofence evaluation
description: The backend forwards new location pings to the geofencing engine. If full-precision coordinates, persistent user identifiers, or unnecessary contextual attributes are sent when coarser location, pseudonymous identifiers, or reduced context would suffice for zone entry/exit checks, the source causes avoidable disclosure of personal data.
assumptions: Location pings relate to identifiable or reasonably linkable users/devices, and geofence evaluation may not require all attributes currently forwarded.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen as best-fit for unnecessary disclosure/minimization at the source; exact subnode may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Location pings in transit can directly identify a user or device
description: The flow carries fresh location pings from P1 to P2. If the payload includes direct identifiers such as account IDs, device IDs, phone numbers, or stable tokens, interception or observation of the flow can identify the data subject associated with the location data.
assumptions: The flow contains stable identifiers or other identifying fields alongside location data.
uncertainty_note: Applies if identifiers are present on the wire; if the flow is strongly pseudonymized and protected, likelihood may be lower.

title: Repeated location pings enable linkage of movements across time
description: Even if each individual ping seems innocuous, repeated transmission of stable identifiers, consistent pseudonyms, or recognizable movement patterns can allow records on this flow to be linked together into a travel history for the same person or device.
assumptions: Multiple pings over time are sent for the same subject and include a stable or quasi-stable correlator, or trajectories themselves are distinctive.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode may differ depending on whether linkage is via explicit identifiers, pseudonyms, or trajectory uniqueness.

title: Geofencing engine can infer sensitive habits or presence from received location streams
description: By processing incoming location pings to determine zone entry/exit, the destination may infer additional personal information beyond the raw coordinates, such as home/work locations, routines, visits to sensitive places, or presence within monitored areas. These inferences may be privacy-invasive if not strictly necessary or properly constrained.
assumptions: P2 retains or analyzes enough location history or zone context to derive behavioral patterns or sensitive place visits.
uncertainty_note: Inference depends on retention, analytics, and the nature of configured zones; exact node is best-fit.

title: Users may be unaware that location pings are repurposed for geofence monitoring and alerts
description: When P2 receives backend location pings for zone entry/exit checks, the data may be processed for continuous monitoring or alerting in ways users do not expect from merely sharing location with the app. If this downstream use is not transparent and consented to where required, the destination creates a non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Applicable where notice, consent, purpose limitation, or lawful-basis requirements apply to geofencing/alert processing.
uncertainty_note: This is a genuine privacy threat only if transparency, consent, or purpose-limitation controls are insufficient in the actual system.

title: Store discloses more location-context data than necessary to the geofencing engine
description: The Family Account & Permissions Store shares configured zone definitions such as home, school, and friend's house with the Geofencing & Alert Engine. These zones reveal highly sensitive location context and social relationships. If DS2 provides full addresses, precise coordinates, labels, or all family zones when only a subset or less precise representation is needed for geofence evaluation, the disclosure is avoidable and violates data minimization.
assumptions: Zone definitions contain personal data because they encode places associated with a child/family and may include semantic labels. The engine may not need all attributes or all zones for every evaluation.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected as a best-fit minimization/disclosure node; exact sub-node may vary by LINDDUN Pro catalog version.

title: Geofencing engine may retain or further use zone definitions beyond immediate evaluation needs
description: Upon receiving configured zones from DS2, the Geofencing & Alert Engine could cache, log, replicate, or reuse the zone definitions for purposes beyond geofence computation and alerting. Because the data reveals habitual locations and relationships, unnecessary retention or secondary use at P2 constitutes avoidable disclosure.
assumptions: P2 may persist operational logs, caches, or telemetry containing zone definitions or derived sensitive place information.
uncertainty_note: Exact Dd sub-node is approximate; grounded in unnecessary onward disclosure/retention at the destination.

title: Zone definitions enable linkage of multiple events to the same family or child
description: The destination process can use stable zone identifiers, labels, or coordinates from the Family Account Store to correlate multiple location events, alerts, and behavioral patterns over time to the same household or child. This creates a linkage risk because repeated processing against the same configured places can tie otherwise separate observations together.
assumptions: P2 has access to recurring event streams or alert histories and zone definitions are stable over time.
uncertainty_note: Specific linkage sub-node is best-effort based on standard LINDDUN linkage patterns.

title: Configured places can identify the child or family
description: Named or precise configured zones such as home, school, and friend's house can directly or indirectly identify a specific child or family when processed by the Geofencing & Alert Engine. Even without explicit names, the combination of a home address and school location may uniquely single out the data subject.
assumptions: Zone definitions include precise coordinates, addresses, or human-readable labels; P2 can access account context or other operational data.
uncertainty_note: Exact I sub-node may differ across catalog versions, but identifiability from location/place data clearly applies.

title: Zone definitions reveal sensitive habits and relationships
description: Processing configured zones such as home, school, and friend's house allows the destination to infer daily routines, likely age group, social ties, and other private aspects of the child's life. These inferences arise from the semantics of the places themselves, even before any live location events are matched against them.
assumptions: Place labels are meaningful and correspond to real-world sensitive locations associated with a child/family.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node is approximate; the core issue is detectability/discoverability of sensitive private information from the received place data.

title: Notification discloses the child's location event to the parent beyond strict necessity
description: The geofencing engine intentionally shares personal data with the parent: that the child entered or exited a defined zone, and implicitly the timing and approximate whereabouts associated with that zone. If the notification includes more detail than needed (e.g., exact timestamp, precise zone label such as home/school, repeated alerts, or additional context), the source's act of sending it creates an avoidable disclosure.
assumptions: Assumes the alert contains personal data about the child and may include zone identity and time of event.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-judgement for explicit disclosure/minimisation; exact subnode may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Alert messages can link repeated zone events to the same child-parent pair
description: Even if alert payloads are limited, the flow itself carries recurring event messages between the same process and parent. Over time, these messages can be correlated to build a pattern of the child's movements and routines, linking multiple events to the same data subject and household.
assumptions: Assumes alerts are recurring and distinguishable as belonging to the same child/account.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode is best-judgement; linkage here is primarily through repeated event correlation on the flow.

title: Zone-entry/exit alerts may identify the child through direct or indirect identifiers in transit
description: The notification may contain direct identifiers (child name, account id, device id) or indirect identifiers (specific zone names, school/home labels, unique timing patterns) that allow the child to be identified from the message in transit.
assumptions: Assumes the alert payload or metadata contains identifiers or sufficiently distinctive contextual data.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-judgement because the retrieved context did not include the identification subtree.

title: Parent can infer sensitive habits and routines from received geofence alerts
description: On receipt, the parent can derive additional personal information from the sequence of arrival/departure notifications, such as attendance patterns, daily schedule, social activities, or visits to sensitive places. This goes beyond the raw event itself and creates a detectability/inference risk at the destination.
assumptions: Assumes alerts are retained or repeatedly observed over time and zones may correspond to meaningful places.
uncertainty_note: This is framed as a detectability/inference-style privacy risk at the destination; exact subtree citation may differ across LINDDUN Pro versions.

title: Parent may receive or use geofence alerts without the child's awareness or meaningful transparency
description: The destination receives location-event notifications about the child, but the child may not be aware when alerts are generated, what exact data is shared, or how long the parent can retain and use the information. This creates an unawareness threat tied to the recipient's receipt and subsequent use of the data.
assumptions: Assumes the child is a data subject distinct from the parent recipient and lacks clear notice about alerting behavior.
uncertainty_note: Best-judgement subtree id; the core issue is lack of transparency/awareness rather than security.

title: Parent may disclose more child data than necessary during registration
description: The registration flow includes child name, date of birth, school, and geofence definitions. Entering and transmitting this full set at account creation can expose excessive personal data about the child if all fields are not strictly necessary for initial service setup.
assumptions: Assumes some attributes or geofence details may be optional or not required at registration time.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort because the retrieved context did not include detailed threat-tree nodes.

title: Child and parent can be identified from registration data in transit
description: The flow carries direct identifiers and quasi-identifiers, including child name, date of birth, school, and parent account-registration data. Even in transit, these data can identify the child and parent if intercepted or exposed through transport metadata/logging.
assumptions: Assumes transport or intermediary components could expose payload or metadata.
uncertainty_note: Specific node id is approximate; applicability of identification is strong.

title: Registration payload enables linkage of child identity, school, and location context
description: Combining child profile fields with geofence zones allows records about the same child or household to be linked across contexts such as identity, education, and habitual locations. This linkage risk exists for the transmitted dataset as a whole, not only for each field separately.
assumptions: Assumes the backend or intermediaries can correlate these attributes with other records or repeated submissions.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate due to missing detailed mapping in retrieved context.

title: Backend may collect and retain overly detailed child profile and geofence data
description: On receipt, the backend may process or store precise child profile data and geofence definitions beyond what is necessary for the stated purpose. Geofence zones can reveal sensitive habitual places such as home, school, or caregivers' locations.
assumptions: Assumes backend persists the submitted profile and geofence configuration.
uncertainty_note: Threat applies if minimisation controls are absent; exact node id is best-effort.

title: Parent may be insufficiently informed about downstream use of child profile and geofence data
description: If the backend does not clearly explain how child identity data, school information, and geofence zones will be used, retained, shared, or combined for alerts and analytics, the parent may be unaware of the privacy consequences of registration.
assumptions: Assumes transparency notices are incomplete or not presented at the point of collection.
uncertainty_note: Specific tree-node id is approximate; threat depends on notice quality.

title: Collection of child data and geofence information may lack valid consent or appropriate child-data legal basis
description: The backend receives personal data about a child, including potentially sensitive location-related geofence information. If the service does not obtain and record valid parental authorization, age-appropriate notices, and any required jurisdiction-specific child-data permissions, the processing may be non-compliant.
assumptions: Assumes applicable law requires parental authorization and specific safeguards for children's data.
uncertainty_note: Legal obligations vary by jurisdiction; exact node id is approximate.

title: Backend may be unable to demonstrate what privacy notice and permissions were accepted at registration
description: If the backend does not keep adequate evidence of the parent's registration actions, presented notices, and consent or authorization choices, it may be difficult to prove what was agreed regarding the child's profile and geofence processing.
assumptions: Assumes the system relies on consent/authorization or notice acknowledgement during registration.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation relevance depends on whether consent or notice acknowledgement is part of this flow.

title: Backend stores more child and geofence data than strictly necessary
description: The backend sends account data, child profiles, and geofence zone data to the permissions store. If all attributes, historical values, or precise location-related zone definitions are persisted by default rather than only the minimum needed for account and permission management, the act of sharing this dataset causes avoidable disclosure of personal data to storage.
assumptions: Assumes DS2 is used for account and permission management and does not strictly require every child-profile field or full geofence detail sent by P1.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement for excessive collection/storage under Data Disclosure; exact sub-node may vary by LINDDUN Pro catalog version.

title: Stored child profile and geofence data may be retained or exposed beyond the intended purpose
description: On receipt, the data store may keep account, child, and geofence information in a form or for a duration broader than necessary for family-account permissions. Because these data concern children and location-related zones, unnecessary persistence or broad internal availability at the destination increases avoidable disclosure risk.
assumptions: Assumes DS2 persists the received data and may support broader querying, replication, backup retention, or secondary use.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree sub-node is approximate; grounded in destination-side unnecessary storage/availability of sensitive personal data.

title: Family account records can link child identities, guardians, and geofence zones
description: By storing account data, child profiles, and geofence zone data together, the destination can create or strengthen associations between multiple family members, their roles, and location-related settings. This enables linkage of records that may reveal household structure and relationships beyond what individual data items reveal alone.
assumptions: Assumes DS2 stores these data under shared account identifiers or otherwise correlatable keys.
uncertainty_note: Sub-node chosen by best judgement for record/linkage creation at the destination.

title: Stored family and geofence data can identify specific children or households
description: The combination of account identifiers, child profile attributes, and geofence zone information may directly identify a child, parent, or household, or make them identifiable when combined with other data already present in the store. The identification risk arises at the destination because DS2 receives and persists the combined dataset.
assumptions: Assumes child profiles contain names, birthdays, avatars, device identifiers, or other quasi-identifiers, and geofence zones are specific enough to point to home, school, or routine locations.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node is approximate; this is a standard destination-side identifiability risk from combined personal data.

title: Future use of stored child and geofence data may exceed the original purpose
description: Once stored in the family account and permissions datastore, the received data may later be queried or reused for analytics, profiling, feature expansion, or operational purposes not originally expected by users. This creates an unawareness risk because data subjects may not understand that child-profile and geofence information are being kept in a permissions store for broader downstream use.
assumptions: Assumes privacy notices or in-app explanations may not clearly describe all storage purposes and downstream uses of these data.
uncertainty_note: Threat depends on transparency and purpose-specification controls not visible from the DFD alone.

title: Storage of child profile and geofence data may conflict with data-minimization and child-privacy obligations
description: Persisting child-related profile data together with geofence zone information in a permissions datastore may violate privacy requirements if the system stores more data than necessary, lacks a clear lawful basis, or fails to apply heightened protections expected for children's and location-related data. The compliance risk materializes at the destination where the data are stored and managed.
assumptions: Assumes the system is subject to privacy obligations such as purpose limitation, storage limitation, transparency, and special protections for children's/location data.
uncertainty_note: Compliance obligations are jurisdiction-dependent; exact legal basis cannot be inferred from the DFD alone.

title: Parent request contains identified account context
description: The parent's request to view a child's current or historical location is typically tied to an authenticated parent account and a specific child profile. By sending this request, the source discloses identified data about the requester-child relationship to the backend.
assumptions: Assumes the request includes or is bound to an authenticated parent identity and a selected child account/device.

title: Request metadata can link parent and child over time
description: Even if the payload is minimized, the flow metadata can reveal that a particular parent account repeatedly requests location data for a particular child. This can enable linking of records and sessions over time, exposing the parent-child association and behavioral patterns.
assumptions: Assumes transport or application-layer metadata, identifiers, session tokens, or stable account references are observable within system components handling the flow.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement; retrieved context did not include a more specific linkability node.

title: Location-view request reveals sensitive behavioral intent in transit
description: The fact that the parent is requesting current location or location history may disclose private information such as monitoring behavior, concern about the child's whereabouts, and the existence of a child-tracking relationship. The request itself therefore carries sensitive contextual information beyond its explicit payload.
assumptions: Assumes intermediaries, logs, or network-observable metadata can infer the nature and timing of the request.
uncertainty_note: Specific disclosure node is approximate because the retrieved context did not provide disclosure subtree details.

title: Backend learns and may retain sensitive location-access patterns
description: On receipt of the request, the backend can infer when and how often a parent checks a child's current or historical location. These access patterns may reveal family routines, suspicion, emergencies, or other sensitive circumstances if processed or retained beyond what is necessary.
assumptions: Assumes the backend logs, profiles, analyzes, or stores request history.
uncertainty_note: Specific disclosure node is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the relevant disclosure subtree.

title: Backend may process the request for secondary purposes without parent awareness
description: The backend may use incoming location-view requests not only to serve the map but also for analytics, profiling, feature optimization, or monitoring of parental behavior. If these purposes are not transparent to the parent, the processing can be unexpected.
assumptions: Assumes secondary use of request data or logs beyond the immediate service purpose.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected by best judgement; retrieved context did not include unawareness subtree details.

title: Backend processing may exceed or mismatch communicated consent/expectations
description: If the backend processes or stores the parent's location-view request history in ways not covered by the applicable consent, parental controls, or privacy notice, the handling of this flow may be non-compliant with stated expectations or legal requirements.
assumptions: Assumes there are purpose, retention, or transparency constraints on handling requests for child location data.
uncertainty_note: Specific non-compliance node is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the Nc subtree.

title: Excessive disclosure of location history from store
description: The location history store may return more location data than is strictly necessary for the parent's requested map/history view, such as an overly broad time range, unnecessarily precise coordinates, or records for additional subjects. This creates avoidable disclosure of sensitive personal data when the store shares the data with the backend.
assumptions: Assumes the backend request or datastore query could retrieve broader history than needed for the specific UI request.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimality patterns; exact subnode may vary by catalog version.

title: Disclosure of sensitive location history in transit
description: Location history is highly sensitive personal data. If this flow is insufficiently protected in transit or exposed through logs, traces, message inspection, or internal network monitoring, the transfer itself can disclose a child's historical whereabouts to unauthorized parties.
assumptions: Assumes this retrieval traverses a boundary where transport protection, service-mesh policy, or observability tooling may expose payloads or metadata.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is approximate; threat applicability is strong even if the subnode label differs in the local LINDDUN tree.

title: Backend may use retrieved location history beyond the parent's expected purpose
description: After receiving stored location history to render the parent's map/history view, the backend could also use the same data for secondary purposes such as analytics, profiling, feature experimentation, or operational reuse not aligned with the user's expectation for this retrieval. This creates an unawareness threat if such use is not transparent to the data subjects and parent.
assumptions: Assumes the system privacy notice or in-product explanation may not clearly communicate all downstream uses of retrieved history.
uncertainty_note: Subnode id is best-effort; the core issue is lack of transparency about downstream use at the destination.

title: Backend retrieval may be incompatible with consent or parental-choice constraints
description: The backend's access to stored location history may conflict with consent, retention, or parental-control choices if it retrieves data outside the scope currently permitted, for example after consent withdrawal, outside configured history windows, or for a child/account not covered by valid authorization. This is a non-compliance risk at the receiving process.
assumptions: Assumes consent/authorization/retention constraints exist for location-history access and must be enforced at retrieval time.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate because the provided context does not include the detailed non-compliance subtree.

title: Parent may disclose the child's location-sharing relationship to an unintended or wrong secondary guardian
description: By initiating an invitation for a secondary guardian, the parent causes personal data about the child and the parent-child relationship to be shared onward. If the parent selects the wrong recipient, mistypes contact details, or invites someone without proper authority, the act of sharing itself discloses that the child is being tracked and that the parent is associated with the child.

description: Once the backend receives the invitation request, it may create or send an invitation that grants or prepares access for a secondary guardian. If authorization checks are weak, consent is not properly validated, or invitation redemption is insecure, the backend's processing can disclose the child's location data to someone who should not receive it.

title: Live-location flow can identify the child and guardian relationship in transit
description: The transmission of live location from the backend to the secondary guardian can directly or indirectly identify the child, and reveal that a specific adult is associated with that child as a guardian. Even if payload fields are minimized, traffic contents or associated metadata may enable identification.

description: Because this flow shares live location, successive transmissions can be linked together to build a movement history for the child. The same flow may also link the child to the secondary guardian through recurring access patterns and communication metadata.
assumptions: Assumes live location is shared repeatedly or continuously rather than as a one-off coarse location.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node id is approximate.

title: Secondary guardian may further disclose the child's live location beyond the intended purpose
description: Once received, the secondary guardian can store, screenshot, relay, or otherwise share the child's live location with others, causing an additional disclosure beyond the original intended recipient and purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the external entity is outside direct technical control of the system and may retain or onward-share received data.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node id is approximate.

title: Secondary guardian may use live location for purposes not expected by the child or primary guardian
description: The recipient may use the child's live location for monitoring, profiling routines, or other secondary purposes that are not transparent to the child or aligned with the original purpose of access.
assumptions: Assumes purpose limitation is not technically enforced once data reaches the external recipient.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node id is approximate.

title: Granting secondary-guardian access without valid consent or legal basis may be non-compliant
description: Sharing a child's live location is highly sensitive processing. If the backend grants access without obtaining, recording, or honoring the required parental authorization, consent, or other legal basis, the disclosure may violate applicable privacy obligations.
assumptions: Assumes the service is subject to consent, child-protection, or purpose-limitation requirements for location sharing.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node id is approximate and legal applicability depends on jurisdiction and service context.

title: Backend discloses analytics data to a third-party partner beyond users' expectations
description: By sending usage and engagement analytics to an external advertising/analytics partner, the backend discloses information about users' behavior to a third party. Even if described as aggregated, the act of sharing can still reveal information about user cohorts, feature usage, geography, or time-based behavior that users may not expect to be shared for monetization purposes.
assumptions: The shared analytics contains information derived from user behavior and is not purely anonymous in a mathematically robust sense.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include detailed threat-tree nodes.

title: Partner may link received analytics with its existing datasets
description: The advertising/analytics partner may combine the received aggregated usage and engagement analytics with other datasets it already holds, enabling linkage across apps, campaigns, regions, time periods, or customer segments. This can increase the ability to single out or profile groups and potentially re-associate data with identifiable users or devices when combined with auxiliary information.
assumptions: EE4 operates multiple analytics or advertising services and has access to additional datasets that can be correlated with the received analytics.
uncertainty_note: Applies especially if aggregation granularity is fine or partner receives persistent campaign/app identifiers; exact tree node is approximate.

title: Partner may infer identities or identifiable segments from aggregated analytics
description: If the shared analytics is broken down by narrow cohorts, geography, device type, timestamp, campaign, or other dimensions, the partner may infer the identity of individuals or very small groups, especially when combined with external knowledge. Aggregation alone does not guarantee non-identifiability.
assumptions: The analytics includes dimensions or low-count segments that permit singling out or narrowing to identifiable persons.
uncertainty_note: Identification risk depends strongly on aggregation thresholds and whether small-cell suppression or differential privacy is used.

title: Partner may use analytics for secondary purposes beyond funding the free tier
description: Once received, the partner may retain, analyze, enrich, or repurpose the analytics for advertising optimization, audience modeling, benchmarking, product improvement, or onward sharing, beyond the original stated purpose of funding the app's free tier. This creates a detectability/disclosure risk through broader exposure and use of the data.
assumptions: Contractual or technical controls do not strictly limit EE4's downstream use, retention, or onward disclosure.
uncertainty_note: Threat type classification is based on LINDDUN's disclosure of information to unintended parties / broader exposure concept; exact node is approximate.

title: Sharing analytics with an advertising partner may occur without valid user consent or other appropriate legal basis
description: Using behavioral analytics for advertising/monetization purposes may require consent or another valid legal basis depending on jurisdiction and the nature of the data. If the backend shares analytics without obtaining and honoring the required permissions or preferences, the flow creates a non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Applicable law or platform policy requires consent, opt-out, or transparency for this type of third-party analytics/advertising sharing.
uncertainty_note: Legal applicability varies by jurisdiction and whether the data is truly anonymous.

title: Users may be unaware that their app usage contributes to third-party advertising analytics
description: Users may not understand that their engagement data is shared with an external advertising/analytics partner to subsidize the free tier, especially if notices are vague or bundled. This undermines users' ability to make informed choices about the processing.
assumptions: Privacy notices or in-app disclosures do not clearly explain the partner sharing and monetization purpose.
uncertainty_note: This threat is strongest where disclosures are generic or buried in privacy documentation.

title: Flow metadata may enable linkage between the app backend and partner datasets
description: Even if payload data is aggregated, the transmission itself may carry stable app, account, campaign, tenant, or reporting identifiers, as well as timing and frequency patterns. These metadata can help the partner link successive reports together and correlate them with other datasets.
assumptions: The flow includes stable identifiers or consistent metadata across transmissions.
uncertainty_note: Applies primarily if transport- or application-level metadata is visible and stable across reports.

title: Child discloses precise real-time location in SOS/check-in
description: By sending a manual check-in or SOS, the child shares highly sensitive personal data: their current location together with the fact that they initiated an SOS/check-in. This reveals whereabouts and potentially current circumstances to the receiving system.
assumptions: The message contains precise or near-real-time location and is associated with the child's account.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is based on general LINDDUN disclosure taxonomy; exact sub-node may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Child is identifiable from account-linked SOS/check-in
description: The SOS/check-in message is likely tied to the child's account, device, or parent-child relationship, making the child directly or indirectly identifiable when sending the message and location.
assumptions: The backend can associate the message with a specific child profile, device identifier, or authenticated session.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id may differ depending on whether the threat tree distinguishes direct vs indirect identifiability.

title: SOS/check-in transmissions can be linked over time
description: Repeated check-in/SOS messages on this flow can be linked to the same child through stable identifiers, session metadata, network metadata, or recurring location patterns, enabling reconstruction of movement and behavior over time.
assumptions: The flow carries stable account/device/session identifiers or otherwise exposes consistent metadata.
uncertainty_note: Specific sub-node for linkability via content vs metadata is not available in the retrieved context.

title: Location and emergency context may be exposed in transit
description: The data flow contains sensitive content: current location and the fact that the child is performing a manual check-in or SOS. If transport protections are weak or metadata is observable, this information may be disclosed during transmission.
assumptions: An attacker or intermediary may observe payload or traffic metadata; transport confidentiality may be imperfect.
uncertainty_note: Applies strongly to metadata even when payload encryption is present; payload exposure depends on transport protections.

title: Traffic metadata can identify the child or household in transit
description: Even if message contents are encrypted, traffic metadata such as source IP, device identifiers, timing, and destination can help identify the child, their device, or their household and associate them with use of the child-safety service.
assumptions: Network or application-layer metadata is visible to intermediaries or observers.
uncertainty_note: Exact identifiability depends on network architecture and whether identifiers are exposed outside encrypted channels.

title: Backend stores attributable evidence that the child sent the SOS/check-in
description: On receipt, the backend may log or persist a record showing that a specific child account/device sent a check-in or SOS at a particular time and place. This creates attributable evidence that the child performed the action, reducing plausible deniability.
assumptions: The backend stores message content or event logs tied to account/device identity.

title: Backend can link multiple SOS/check-in events into a movement history
description: By receiving and storing repeated location-bearing messages, the backend can correlate events from the same child over time, building a longitudinal record of routines, movements, and incidents.
assumptions: The backend retains historical events and associates them with the same child profile.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node may vary depending on whether linkage is via identifiers, location patterns, or account records.

title: Backend processing and storage disclose sensitive location and distress information
description: The backend receives and may store precise location plus the fact that the child initiated a check-in or SOS. This creates a concentration of sensitive personal data that could be exposed internally, through misconfiguration, or through later secondary use.
assumptions: The backend stores or makes the event accessible to operators, services, or downstream components.
uncertainty_note: This is a destination-side disclosure risk arising from receipt, storage, and internal access rather than only external breach.

title: Backend may process the child's location for purposes beyond immediate alerting
description: Once received, the backend could use the child's location and SOS/check-in history for analytics, profiling, service improvement, or other secondary purposes not expected by the child at the moment of sending the alert.
assumptions: The service retains and reuses event data beyond real-time delivery to the parent.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on actual backend data-governance practices; included because secondary use is a common destination-side privacy risk.

title: Child may lack sufficient awareness or control over backend handling of SOS/check-in data
description: The child may not be adequately informed about how long the backend stores their location-bearing SOS/check-ins, who can access them, or whether they can delete or limit such records. This undermines transparency and control over processing of highly sensitive data.
assumptions: The child is a data subject with limited visibility into backend retention, sharing, and deletion practices.
uncertainty_note: This is a contextual compliance/privacy-control threat; exact applicability depends on notice, consent, and child-specific governance mechanisms.
